Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student

Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.

It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.

"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.

But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.

When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.

"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."

Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death

Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.

She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September , according to the South African Police Service.

Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.

It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.

South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.

Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa

The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.

But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.

For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.

Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.

"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.

The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.

The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa

According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.

This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".

Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.

Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.

"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".

Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00

Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.

Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.

In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.

Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.

The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.

Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.

Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.

"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."

Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.

Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her

Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.

She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.

When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.

"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.

She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.

Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.

In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.

She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.

Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.

Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles

In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.

She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later .

It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'

Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.

Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.

"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed

Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.

Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.

Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."

This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

MN202611_1e3b60042gu.t:
Maxine Dillion says she needed help to get through her to-do list

Maxine Dillion, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores.

Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it.

"I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media.

Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry.

Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic.

Maxine, who earns £32,000 a year, doesn't have a massive amount of disposable income, but she decided to start spending £250 a month for five hours' work and thinks it is worth it as it also helps reduce her "mental load" .

The owners of Life Laundry, Alicia Papachristou and Jane Forbes, now look after a host of things for Maxine. Other jobs they take care of include arranging insurance, sending school emails, and managing online subscriptions.

Much of the work they can do remotely, but once a month they travel to Mansfield to do the jobs that require them to be physically present.

"If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes.

Amanda says she and her husband made a conscious decision to spend more quality time with their family

With such companies also increasingly available in the US, another busy working mother, Amanda Sims Nichols in Austin, Texas, has also employed a firm to look after her life admin.

Amanda, who is a business consultant, has three children with her attorney husband, and decided to start paying for help with life admin after moving house, away from her family support network.

She pays $2,250 (£1,750) a month for 25 hours, and says she relishes offloading regular chores including the weekly food shop and clothes washing.

"Money cannot buy you everything, but it can buy you back some of your time," says the 45-year-old.

The company she uses, Queen of To Do, was founded by Kate Ginsberg in 2011. She says that interest has greatly increased since the pandemic.

The business now has more than 50 active users. Meanwhile, Life Laundry has 25 customers.

Both companies say demand is growing for their services as people's lives become increasingly frantic.

Ginsberg says that the work they do for clients can be very diverse, with no task too big or too small.

Some of the larger tasks her team has faced over the years include flying from Austin to New York City to buy a desperately needed Christmas gift, and finding a new wedding location for a client with just three days' notice due to an incoming hurricane.

Staff of life admin companies will do most jobs around the house for a client

Jess Baker, a UK chartered psychologist, says the appeal of such providers is understandable.

"Using a life PA, if you can afford one, takes the pressure off having to keep hundreds of to-dos swimming around your head, or on lists you might forget to look at," she says.

"Otherwise, the cognitive load can lead to feelings of being overwhelmed, excess worry and exhaustion."

While paying for help with such tasks may seem a luxury, for some people support with life's everyday trials is a lifeline.

Anna Allington sought help after her husband died. "My husband passed away. I was 47," she says.

"And the same week he passed away, I got leukaemia. There was a lot to sort out and I was very, very unwell."

Anna, now 51, still suffers the after-effects of her cancer. "I can't function executively like I used to," she says.

She pays £1,200 a month for 40 hours of help from Cheshire-based company Vi-Va. Her personal assistant helps her respond to emails, manage her diary and make travel plans and bookings.

"We meet twice a week on Zoom," says Anna, who lives in the Cotswolds, so they can go through all her tasks.

Many of us would love for someone else to do our laundry

Many more women than men use these companies.

Queen of To Do says just 20% of its clients are male, while only one of Life Laundry's 25 clients is a man.

Some of that disparity is likely due to mothers still looking after the lion's share of household admin, as studies continue to show.

However, Life Laundry's Forbes wonders if some men are too proud to ask for assistance.

"Men are struggling as well, but I think they're less likely to ask for help."

Ayana Bailey says she relies on her mum to go through the job application process with her

Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her.

"It's not like there's going to be a target on my back, but I'm just like, 'maybe they won't select me'," says Bailey, a part-time florist.

A British Dyslexia Association (BDA) survey of more than 1,200 working dyslexic adults found Bailey isn't alone - with 46% hiding their dyslexia at work.

Some 81% believe the condition adds to their work-related stress.

Bailey was diagnosed aged 11 and says she received good support at school, including mentoring, which helped her to understand her strengths and manage low self-esteem.

But the world of work has proved more challenging.

For Bailey, the application process is "daunting". She says she relies on her mum to go through it with her.

In interviews, Bailey says: "I just shut down. I completely forget who I am."

One way of coping, she says, is to have a little script, but she admits it doesn't always work.

Bailey, who studied film and wants to go into the creative arts, says that while dyslexia has sometimes made her feel anxious, it's also given her opportunities.

"I would definitely say my creativity and thinking outside the box [is my biggest strength]."

She says her dyslexia makes her a visual learner - able to imagine characters before seeing any written descriptions and helping her dream of becoming a casting director.

For nurse Lisa Daniels, her dyslexia meant leaving work more than an hour late most days just to finish the paperwork.

"I suppressed it. I was like 'Oh no, everything is fine. It's not affecting me.'" In reality, she says "it was majorly affecting me".

Daniels, 37, says a previous manager was dismissive of her request for adjustments.

"When I first started, they said, 'Oh they are babying some of these nurses' and I didn't have the confidence to challenge it."

Lisa Daniels says she has built up her resilience despite previous bad experiences at work

She says her suggestions of having more accessible fonts and colours on documents were not listened to.

Five years into her career, Daniels' colleague told her about a staff network on neurodiversity and her confidence grew, along with adjustments such as noise-cancelling headphones.

"I have that resilience that, despite the sometimes lack of support, I'm still gonna show up. I'm still gonna try."

Daniels says she's now recovered from her imposter syndrome.

Why I stopped hiding my dyslexia at work

Over half of people surveyed by the BDA say dyslexia makes them feel bad about themselves, while 39% have experienced bad mental health related to it.

The BDA is calling for workplaces to make reasonable adjustments for employees who need them, even without a diagnosis, and wants managers to be trained to understand and support dyslexic employees.

Its report finds dyslexic employees often have to put extra effort into work, finding their own ways to cope if systems, processes and communication are not accessible.

There are 3.3 million dyslexic adults currently in employment, estimates the BDA. Some told the report:

"I have to cope with little comments that are seen as banter about my spelling."

"My line manager is actually dyslexic and we happily talk about it. We share best practice and war stories."

"It would be nice to be seen as intellectual. Just because I cannot always write as well as others, doesn't mean I don't have the knowledge."

"I revealed my dyslexia quite early on in my employment… I do believe it was used as a stick to beat me with."

"I feel like I have got to do more, be more, show more... because I've got this deficit of being dyslexic".

Employment law solicitor Jenna Ide helped a client win a high-profile dyslexia discrimination case against Starbucks in 2016.

"Many dyslexic employees start a new job already struggling with low self-esteem," she says.

"That's especially true of dyslexics who are late-diagnosed and who may have spent years at school and in earlier jobs believing they just weren't clever enough.

"When an employer doesn't understand dyslexia, relies on inaccessible ways of working and doesn't offer support, it reinforces those feelings and can make people more reluctant to ask for help."

Kate Griggs, founder of UK charity Made By Dyslexia, agrees recruitment can still be a barrier, particularly when it is skewed toward written applications and timed tests.

"My advice to young dyslexics is simple: know your strengths, own them and talk about them with confidence. Ask for the support you need and different ways to show what you can do. Find the roles where those strengths are valued."

Lawyer Jenna Ide represented a client in a high-profile dyslexia discrimination case

Ellen Broomé, head of the British Dyslexia Association, said: "Dyslexic people should not have to work harder simply to have the same opportunities as their colleagues.

"Our research reveals the hidden cost many pay, spending additional time and energy compensating for workplaces that fail to understand or support them.

"This is not a question of ability, ambition or talent. It is about the barriers people face and the opportunities lost when workplaces fail to recognise and support different ways of thinking and working."

MN202611_9kvjjts6mv.t: Umunyamabanga mukuru wa OTAN, Mark Rutte, yatangaje ko uru runani rwiteguriye guhangana n’ico cose coza kibangamira umutekano w’ikirere c’ibihugu birugize, inyuma y’amakuru avuga ko Uburusiya bushobora kuba buriko burategura kurungika mu kirere ikigendajuru igifise ibirwanisho ruhonyanganda vy’ubumara (canke vya nikleyeri). Ibinyamakuru vyo mu Budagi vyatangaje ko amakuru y’igendereza yasangijwe ibihugu bigize OTAN yerekana ko Uburusiya bushobora kurungika ico kigendajuru mu misi 60 iri imbere. Amakuru yatangajwe n’ibinyamakuru vyo mu Budagi, NDR na WDR, hamwe n’ikinyamakuru Sueddeutsche Zeitung, yisunze amasoko yo mu gisirikare no mu nzego z’igendereza atashimye ko amazina yayo amenyekana avuga ko ico kigendajuru kizwi nka Sputnik-S, coba gifise umutwe ufise ibiturika vya nikleyeri ushobora guhungabanya canke gusambura ibindi bigendajuru bikoreshwa mw’itumatumanako no mu kugenzura ibikorwa bitandukanye kw’isi. Rutte yabwiye abanyamakuru i Berlin ko OTAN izobandanya gukingira “buri gace k’ubutaka bw’abayigize”, harimwo n’umutekano wo mu kirere. Arahumuriza kandi ko uru runani rufise uburyo butandukanye bwo kwivuna igitero ico ari co cose. Ku ruhande rw’Uburusiya, umuvugizi wa Kremlin (ibiro vy’umukuru w’igihugu), Dmitry Peskov, yamiriye kure ayo makuru, avuga ko ashingiye ku masoko atazwi, ubuserukizi bw’Uburusiya i Berlin na bwo bukaba buvuga ko ayo makuru atagira ishingiro kandi ko ari ugushikuza. Umukuru wa reta y’Ubudagi, Friedrich Merz, ntiyemeje canke ngo ahakane ayo makuru, ariko yavuze ko yerekana urugero rw’ukuntu Uburusiya bushobora gutuma ibintu vyunyuka. Hagati aho, umukuru w’ikigo ca Buraya gijejwe ikirere (ESA), Josef Aschbacher, yavuze ko gushira ibirwanisho vya nikleyeri mu kirere vyoba ari “ikintu giteye ubwoba kuruta ibindi vyose.” Aya makuru yongeye kuvyura impari zijanye n’iyubahirizwa ry’Amasezerano yo mu 1967 abuza kurungika ibirwanisho ruhonyanganda vy’ubumara mu kirere. Mu 2024, Amerika na yo yari yagirije Uburusiya ko bwariko buhingura ikirwanisho ca nikleyeri co gusambura ibindi bigendajuru, ariko bwarabihakanye. Ayandi makuru ushobora gusoma: Uburusiya buriko buhingura ikirwanisho ‘giteye ubwoba’ gisambura ibigendajuru – bivugwa na Amerika Uburusiya bwatangaje ko bwagerageje igisasu cya misile kirimbuzi kivuduka kurusha ijwi

Minisitiri w’Imari n’Igenamigambi, Yusuf Murangwa, yatangaje ko ivugurura ririmo gukorwa mu mikorere y’Umurenge SACCO rimaze gutanga umusaruro, aho igipimo cy’inguzanyo zitishyurwa neza cyagabanutse kikava kuri 9% kikagera kuri 3%.

Yabigarutseho ku wa 23 Ugushyingo 2026, ubwo yitabaga Komisiyo ihoraho y’Inteko Ishinga Amategeko ishinzwe Ubukungu n’Ubucuruzi, kugira ngo asubize ibibazo by’abadepite ku ivugurura ririmo gukorwa mu mikorere y’Umurenge SACCO.

Iri vugurura riri mu rwego rwo guhindura imikorere y’izi koperative zo kwizigama no kugurizanya, hagamijwe kuzinoza no kuzongerera ubushobozi kugira ngo zirusheho gutanga serivisi z’imari zinoze ku banyamuryango bazo.

Imwe mu mpinduka ziri muri iri vugurura ni uguhuza Umurenge SACCO zo mu mirenge zigakorera hamwe ku rwego rw’Akarere. Ibi bigamije kunoza imikorere yazo, koroshya imiyoborere no gutuma serivisi zihabwa abanyamuryango zirushaho kuba nziza.

Guhuza izi SACCO kandi biri mu ngamba zigamije koroshya uburyo abaturage bagerwaho na serivisi z’imari, guteza imbere ikoreshwa ry’ikoranabuhanga no kurushaho kurinda ubwizigame bw’abanyamuryango.

Ati “Imirenge SACCO ifite uruhare mu gufasha abaturage kwizigamira no kubona inguzanyo zo gukoresha mu bikorwa bitandukanye. Ni yo mpamvu kunoza imikorere yayo bifatwa nk'ingenzi mu gutuma abanyamuryango barushaho kugirira icyizere izi koperative no kuzigirira akamaro”.

Minisitiri Murangwa yavuze ko kugeza ubu inguzanyo Umurenge SACCO imaze gutanga zifite agaciro ka miliyari 200 z’amafaranga y’u Rwanda. Yagaragaje ko muri icyo gihe igipimo cy’inguzanyo zitishyurwa neza cyagabanutse kikava kuri 9% kikagera kuri 3%.

Kugabanuka kw’iki gipimo ni kimwe mu bimenyetso by’uko hari intambwe imaze guterwa mu kunoza imicungire y’inguzanyo zitangwa n’izi SACCO. Iyo inguzanyo zitishyuwe uko bikwiye, bishobora kugira ingaruka ku bushobozi bw’ikigo cy’imari bwo gukomeza gutanga izindi nguzanyo no gufasha abandi banyamuryango.

Nubwo igipimo cy’inguzanyo zitishyurwa neza cyagabanutse, Minisitiri Murangwa yagaragaje ko hakiri imbogamizi zigomba gukemurwa kugira ngo ivugurura rigere ku musaruro urambye.

Mu byo yavuze ko bikwiye gukomeza kunozwa harimo imikorere y’izi SACCO, kongerera ubushobozi abakozi n’abayobozi bazo ndetse no kurushaho kunoza serivisi zihabwa abanyamuryango.

Ati“Kongerera ubushobozi abakozi n’abayobozi ni ingenzi kugira ngo bashobore gucunga neza umutungo w’abanyamuryango, gutanga inguzanyo mu buryo buboneye no gukurikirana uko zisubizwa. Ni na byo bifasha izi koperative gukora kinyamwuga no kurushaho kugira imikorere inoze”.

Ku rundi ruhande, Minisitiri Murangwa yavuze ko kunoza serivisi zihabwa abanyamuryango bisaba ko izi SACCO zirushaho kwita ku byo bakeneye, koroshya uburyo babonamo serivisi no gukoresha ikoranabuhanga mu mikorere yazo.

Minisitiri yagaraje ko iri vugurura risaba gukomeza kunoza imikorere kugira ngo Imurenge SACCO irusheho kuba ibigo by’imari bifite ubushobozi bwo gucunga neza ubwizigame bw’abaturage, gutanga inguzanyo no gutanga serivisi zinoze ku banyamuryango bazo.

Minisitiri Murangwa yagaragaje ko nubwo hari umusaruro umaze kuboneka, hakiri urugendo rwo gukomeza kunoza imikorere y’izi SACCO, kongerera ubushobozi abazicunga no kurushaho guteza imbere serivisi zihabwa abaturage.

Umushinga w’itegeko rigenga ibidukikije n’ihinduka ry’ibihe uteganya ko ibikorwa cyangwa imishinga ishobora kwangiza ibidukikije bizajya bisabwa gutanga ingwate yo kubisana, kugira ngo hirindwe ko ahangijwe n’ibikorwa by’abantu hasigara harangiritse burundu.

Byatangajwe na Minisitiri w’Ibidukikije Dr Bernadette Arakwiye kuri uyu wa mbere tariki 23 Ugushyingo 2026 ageza umushinga w’itegeko rigenga ibidukikije n’ihinduka ry’ibihe mu Rwanda ku Nteko Ishinga Amategeko Umutwe w’Abadepite.

Minisitiri Arakwiye yavuze ko muri uyu mushinga w’itegeko harimo ingingo zigamije gukumira iyangirika ry’ibidukikije no gushyiraho uburyo bwo kubisana nyuma y’uko imishinga cyangwa ibikorwa birangiye. Umushinga w’itegeko ushimangira ko hagomba kwitabwa ku nyungu z’abaturage batuye hafi y’aho ibyo bikorwa bikorerwa.

Minisitiri asobanura ko uyu mushinga ugaragaza ko Iteka rya Minisitiri ari ryo rizagena ibikorwa cyangwa imishinga bizajya bisabwa gutanga iyo ngwate, uburyo agaciro kayo kazabarwa n’uko kazajya gahuzwa n’igihe.

Iyi ngwate izaba igamije gutuma abafite imishinga bashyira mu igenamigambi ryabo amafaranga azifashishwa mu gusana ibidukikije igihe ibikorwa byabo birangiye.

Umushinga kandi uteganya ko uburenganzira bwo gusaba gusubizwa ingwate yo gusana ibidukikije buzajya burangira mu gihe cy’amezi atandatu uhereye igihe byemejwe ko ibikorwa byarangiye.

Izi ngingo ziri mu ngamba zigamije kurinda ko imishinga y’iterambere isiga yangije ibidukikije, ahubwo ko abayishyira mu bikorwa bazajya bagira uruhare mu gusana ahangijwe.

Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space

Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.

Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".

The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".

Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.

"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.

Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".

"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.

A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".

Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation .

"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.

In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

MN202611_1qak5jdd207.t:
Saurav Das said that he was supposed to deliver a series of lectures in the UK

A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.

Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".

It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.

Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests , said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.

He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.

"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," he wrote on X.

A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.

Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.

"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.

Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.

In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .

In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.

The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.

There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.

In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.

In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

MN202611_1xc1du8tb8u.t:
The private jets are operated by Qatar Executive - a subsidiary of the Qatar Airways Group, which is one of Fifa's sponsors

Fifa president Gianni Infantino's globetrotting by private jet since his plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup can be revealed.

BBC Sport found Infantino has taken 39 private flights - the equivalent of one every three days - and visited 32 different countries since the news emerged on 28 July.

Our research found he travelled more than 102,800 air miles and spent just under nine days in the air in the space of 115 days.

Critics have accused of Infantino of using tools only at his disposal as president to aid his campaign for re-election next March.

They questioned whether his re-election campaign may have partly motivated any promises made or support offered during those visits.

Fifa said Infantino had a "statutory duty to maintain and develop good relations between and among Fifa, the confederations, 211 member associations, political bodies, and international organisations".

However, he visited nearly double the 18 countries he did in the same period in 2025.

The initial Times story that revealed Infantino's World Cup plan led to a wave of criticism around the world.

But, as BBC Sport revealed, many observers feel Infantino is now the favourite to be re-elected in the spring after his rivals struggled to find a candidate to run against him until the last moment.

And it appears Infantino has managed to shore up support around the world, with critics suggesting his globetrotting was a key part of that strategy.

There has also been concern about the environmental impact of his extensive travels.

Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - said Infantino's travelling was "part of his campaign".

He told BBC Sport: "The issue here is that Fifa does not have rules on campaign funding, so the president can claim that he's going there on official business when indirectly he's using that to campaign.

"And anyone else running against him very likely will not have the financial means to compete with that."

Infantino's position seemed vulnerable after it emerged he had been devising a plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, in a proposal called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

Before FFE was abandoned, Infantino wrote to all 211 member associations saying they would receive $40m (£30m) if they backed the plan.

Lars-Christer Olsson - a former chief executive of Uefa - told BBC Sport the "important" question was "what does he promise and what are the conditions, as he already did when he promised cash if the members supported his FFE project?"

BBC Sport gleaned the information about where Infantino had been travelling to, and when, from postings on his social media accounts.

The reasons for his travels include holding meetings with football association presidents, opening pitches, meeting politicians and attending confederation gatherings.

The private jets he used are operated by Qatar Executive (QE) - a subsidiary of the Qatar Airways Group, which is one of Fifa's sponsors.

BBC Sport used flight-tracking records and the jet registrations of the Qatar Executive fleet to compile a detailed log of Infantino's flights, totalling at least 39 since the start of August. Fifa did not dispute the figure.

It said "all travel is in line with Fifa's regulations" and there are "rules which establish the framework for flights and travel by any Fifa official".

But Fifa declined to comment on how the use of QE flights impacts on the money available from the Qatar Airways sponsorship for the benefit of global football.

The governing body also declined to comment when asked when Infantino had last taken a commercial flight.

Olsson said: "What do these trips cost and who is paying, which are the implications for the total football community?

"Is he provided with transport in his private campaign with the idea of getting something back in return if he is elected? If Fifa is paying for private jets, would it not be better to invest this money in the member associations?"

Maduro said: "That's again a confusion between his role as president of Fifa and his role as candidate to Fifa presidency."

He said there were no regulations within Fifa on the "use of public money to support their campaign".

"There's no independent authority that controls that, there is no regulation of campaign funding," he said.

Infantino's trips included attending the Caribbean Football Union presidents' meeting and a junior football tournament in the Dominican Republic three weeks after FFE failed.

He then flew to Paris, where he attended the esports World Cup , alongside French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman.

On his Instagram account, Infantino said he had "pledged Fifa's support" for the Pakistan Football Federation president's development plans when he met him in the US in September.

A few days later, he referenced a "wonderful discussion" with the president of the Latvian Football Federation during a visit to Riga, describing him as "my dear friend".

During a visit to Indonesia in October for the final of the Fifa ASEAN Cup, he met presidents from the football federations of Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, Maldives, Mongolia, Myanmar, Pakistan, Philippines, Qatar, Singapore, Thailand and Timor-Leste.

He said: "Having your support and shared passion on this momentous occasion means a great deal and together we will continue driving this game forward."

And during a recent trip to Manila, he performed on stage as part of a quartet called the 'Backache Boys', alongside officials from the Asian Football Confederation, and the football federations of Malaysia and the Philippines.

Gianni Infantino opened a mini-pitch in Anguilla in November

Gianni Infantino visited the Philippines for the ASEAN Football Federation Ordinary Congress

Gianni Infantino in Qatar to oversee preparations for the Fifa U17 World Cup

Based on our log of Infantino's private-jet flights, we calculated he spent 213 hours and 49 minutes in the air, travelling about 102,870 air miles.

For the type of private jet Infantino was using, this would produce an estimated 1,673 tonnes of CO2e emissions.

That's equivalent to the emissions 252 people would accumulate on average in an entire year, according to European Union data , external . These figures are conservative estimates based on average fuel burn rates.

Fifa has also been criticised for expanding the number of teams at World Cups, and hosting them in multiple countries, thereby increasing the amount of travel. The 2026 World Cup was described as the 'most polluting World Cup ever'.

Freddie Daley, from the Cool Down Sport for Climate Action Network, said Infantino's behaviour was "emblematic of Fifa's approach to environmental sustainability under his leadership: total and utter disregard".

"Despite numerous pledges, Fifa has failed to deliver any significant plan on how it will achieve them and has instead gone backwards," he added.

Maduro said Fifa's support for initiatives on climate action - which included being a signatory of the United Nation's Sports for Climate Action Framework - was "window dressing".

Fifa did not directly respond to a question about its justification for the environmental impact caused by Infantino's extensive travelling.

A spokesperson for Fifa said its objectives were to "improve football constantly and promote it globally".

They added: "The Fifa president has a statutory duty to maintain and develop good relations between and among Fifa, the confederations, 211 member associations, political bodies, and international organisations.

"To do that, he travels around the world and attends Fifa's tournaments and events. Mr Infantino is elected until 18 March 2027, when the next Fifa presidential election will take place.

"Fifa has put in place rules which establish the framework for flights and travel by any Fifa official.

"The Fifa president routinely travels around the world for various duties, together with relevant officials, on business and tournament-related matters and strives to visit member associations of Fifa whenever he can.

"Fifa expenses are published in our annual report, and all travel is in line with Fifa's regulations.

"Fifa's money belongs to the 211 member associations and an increased investment to $6.35bn for the upcoming cycle reinforces our unwavering commitment to further supporting football development and access globally."

The goats are grazing just below Flamsteed House, home of the Royal Observatory's famous red time ball

A park in south-east London has taken on some new groundskeepers, and they are more than happy to eat on the job.

A small herd of rare Bagot goats has been brought in to clear a steep, overgrown slope below the Royal Observatory in Greenwich Park, in a trial run by The Royal Parks charity.

Over five days the animals will chomp through tough, woody plants and thorny stems on Castle Hill Bank, a patch that is hard to reach with machinery or by hand.

Visitors can watch them at work until Friday, between 11:00 and 15:30 GMT.

The trial uses conservation grazing, a traditional method in which animals keep dominant vegetation in check, giving other plants room to grow and supporting wildlife.

The Royal Parks is working with Mudchute Park and Farm, on the Isle of Dogs, and the Rare Breeds Survival Trust, with funding from players of People's Postcode Lottery.

Bagots are Britain's oldest native breed of goat, according to the charity. They are small and light-footed, which makes them well suited to steep and uneven ground.

Clare Lanes, Greenwich Park manager, said the view of Flamsteed House above the bank was part of what made the park so special as a Unesco World Heritage Site.

"But it's a very steep bank, and managing vegetation to protect that view is a real challenge," she said.

"We're trialling a traditional approach by bringing in goats to graze, which we hope will help us protect the landscape more sustainably."

Holly, brambles and thorny stems are all on the menu at Castle Hill Bank

She said the approach could also help the charity in its ambition to create climate-resilient parks for future generations as well as making a few visitors smile.

The herd is kept in a paddock with a lean-to shelter and fresh water, and is shepherded on and off site each day.

The goats are being watched over by Tom Davis, farm manager at Mudchute, which has previously worked with The Royal Parks on similar projects in other London parks.

He said the scheme was giving an "incredibly rare breed" an important purpose.

Charlotte Cass, who manages The Royal Parks' Help Nature Thrive project, said the charity was "always looking for exciting ways to support nature" and new ways to manage its eight London parks.

"This project helps create a better, more viable habitat for invertebrates, birds and small mammals in Greenwich Park in the longer term," she said.

Viktor Gyokeres has scored twice in all competitions this season

A Premier League trophy and 21 goals in his debut season and a - on paper things have worked out perfectly for Viktor Gyokeres since his £64m transfer to Arsenal.

But, even with those achievements, it has been a tough start to the current campaign for the 28-year-old striker.

The Swede has started just one Premier League game this season and is yet to score in his eight league appearances.

He has started three games in the Champions League, two in the Carabao Cup, and has scored just twice in 15 games in all competitions. Not the numbers he would have hoped for after last season's glory.

It is not just this season that has seen Gyokeres suitability questioned for Arsenal though.

Even though he scored more than 20 goals in his first season in all competitions as Arsenal ended their 22-year wait for a title, his all-round game had its critics.

It has been near enough a straight battle for the number nine role between Kai Havertz and Gyokeres since the Swedish international signed.

And Gyokeres was thrust into leading the line for Arsenal quicker and more frequently than planned after injury kept Havertz out for long periods last season.

Although the Swede may be the more natural finisher, Havertz's all-round play is considered superior with the German also one of Arteta's most trusted players for big games.

Gyokeres, a "win-now signing", was bought for his ability to find the net but also for how he could open up spaces for his team-mates, something they have praised him for.

But playing with his back to goal and linking up play is not natural to Gyokeres and his failure to hold up the ball or win duels with centre-backs has led to fan frustration.

Arteta has spoken about how the striker has been working on improving his hold-up play and connections, and there were hints of it in the Champions League win over Slavia Prague where Gyokeres assisted the opener and scored the winner in arguably his best game of the season.

Raya to miss Dortmund game but injury 'not serious'

A big reason that Gyokeres is not starting games is that Havertz is fit.

Last season, Havertz suffered with knee and hamstring issues which meant Gyokeres was the only option Arteta had.

Had Havertz been fit, he would have played a lot more and the fact that he started the Champions League final and the key match away at Manchester City in last season's title race back this up.

This season Gyokeres has just six starts and Arteta says that his gametime and situation is similar to other members in the squad.

"We have rotated the team a lot and used the competitions as well to give minutes to players and exposure because they are all starters in my opinion," Arteta said.

"Viktor's case is one of many that they have been in the same situation where they play more in the Premier League or more in the Champions League which is not bad, eh?"

Arteta is open with his players about their standing in the squad and said that Gyokeres has not approached him directly about a lack of minutes.

"We have conversations with every player to make sure that they understand what we are doing and to gather information about the way we are feeling and so far it has been very positive with Viktor and the rest of the team," he said.

The signing of Gyokeres is an interesting one in its own right.

The Arsenal recruitment team had done a lot of due diligence on signing, now Manchester United forward, Benjamin Sesko.

It is understood work on that deal had been done but a change of direction to sign Gyokeres happened after Andrea Berta became Arsenal sporting director.

Some around Arsenal have always thought that Gyokeres is not the usual forward that the Gunners would go for and his predicament of a lack of game time was always likely to happen, even if he did play a big part in them ending their trophy drought.

Gyokeres ended last season with 14 league goals but those strikes actually only won Arsenal two points on their way to winning the league.

That is because, although his penalty in the 1-0 win at Everton was the only goal of the game, Arsenal would have come away with a draw, so that strike factually only accounted for two points and not three.

But Gyokeres did put the Gunners ahead five times last season in the league which shows that, among the frustrating performances, he had plenty of impact.

Max Dowman stole the show with his goal in the 2-0 home win over Everton , when he became the youngest scorer in Premier League history, but it was Gyokeres' goal in the 89th-minute which put Arsenal ahead and although it did not lead to a point score on its own, it set them on the way.

Gyokeres also scored in the 4-1 north London derby win, putting Arsenal ahead when Kolo Muani had equalised after Eberechi Eze's opener.

It is unlikely that Gyokeres will be sold in January as he continues to get games in the Champions League and is a senior player who can score goals in big moments.

But if his lack of minutes in the league continue, Gyokeres, who is a driven and ambitious individual, will not want to be the player who is left out of the starting XI in the long term.

Delia Smith, pictured with fellow campaigner Jake Humphrey, says she feels very strongly about protecting Norfolk

Television cook Delia Smith has joined opponents of a £1.2bn data centre, arguing it would threaten a nature reserve.

Campaigners fear the proposed centre at Keswick, on the edge of Norwich, will create noise pollution and have a negative impact on nearby Marston Marsh.

Smith, honorary life president and former majority shareholder of Norwich City FC, said: "I love Norfolk. You can't be involved in a football club for 55 years without being attached to the people and the beauty of Norfolk. I feel very strongly about it."

But developer Norwich Apex said an ecological impact assessment concluded no effect on the reserve was expected.

Data centres are facilities that store and process vast amounts of data and run the software and online services used by millions of people.

This centre, off the A140 Ipswich Road, would need 150 MW of power to run and would feature 72 chiller units on its roof.

According to planning documents, the building would be about 20m (65ft) high.

A planning appiclation for the centre has been lodged wth South Norfolk Council.

If approved, construction could begin at the end of 2027 and it would be operational by 2028.

What are data centres and are more coming to the East?

Smith, who lives in Suffolk, said: "We haven't got enough water, and data centres use an awful lot of water.

"It's one of the biggest [data centres] and it doesn't do anything for Norfolk. It doesn't do anything for the Norfolk community. Where is the £1.2bn coming from?"

Campaigners have raised concerns about the proposed centre's effect on the nearby Marston Marsh nature reserve

It is hoped the centre will utilise wind energy by connecting to the Hornsea 3 substation nearby.

Smith said: "Renewable energy is going into the grid but it doesn't supply everything now.

"What are you going to do when you have this huge data centre absolutely sucking up energy?"

Other opponents of the plan include broadcaster and entrepreneur Jake Humphrey , who lives nearby.

Matt Tomlinson is worried that nocturnal wildlife including owls and bats will be driven away from the area

Other campaigners include Matt Tomlinson of Yare Valley Meadow Makers, who believes the development will have a "disastrous effect" on nocturnal wildlife.

"On this Marston Marsh site we have nine protected bat species, we have three different owl species and these will all need the quiet conditions to effectively hunt," he said.

"I think this is an awful idea; awful for the wildlife and awful for the people."

In recent days, Labour MP for South Norfolk, Ben Goldsborough, who believes the development would be in the wrong place , has been appointed to a new data centre committee that will scrutinise the government's national policies.

Matt Bartram, chief executive of Norwich Apex, said: "Our ambition is to deliver one of the UK's greenest data centres, using low-carbon power supplied via Norwich Main substation. Protecting nearby ecological sites, including Marston Marshes has shaped the design from the outset.

"Detailed environment assessments have informed our plans to reduce noise and screen the development from view.

"We propose planting more than 15,700 trees and over 1.7km of new hedgerow, with the plans delivering a 13% biodiversity net gain."

MN202611_oe27yb0nw.t:
Sheikh Hasina has been living in exile in India since 2024

Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.

Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.

The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.

But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule . She denies the charges.

Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.

"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.

Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.

India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ​request for comment. In April, ​the ministry said it was ⁠examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".

Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.

What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.

On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.

"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.

The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.

Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.

Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.

The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.

The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.

But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.

Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.

"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.

Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.

India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.

But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.

Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.

The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

MN202611_se31q2vy6w.t:
The first ever Children's Booker Prize has announced the eight books in the running for the new £50,000 award.

Five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories are on the shortlist, which is aimed at children aged eight to 12. The authors in contention include former Children's Laureate of Ireland Eoin Colfer, who is best known for his Artemis Fowl series, and teacher and children's author Catherine Bruton.

Four children have also been announced as new judges after a UK-wide competition.

12-year old Ibrahim from Hampshire was one of those picked from more than 4000 entrants.

He told me he was called back into school for a phone call with chair of judges Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who broke the news. Ibrahim said he couldn't be happier.

"First Children's Booker Prize judge! On my CV - that's going to take me a long way… I'm too overwhelmed to even be excited."

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC "it's really, really important that this is a prize for children's books. Having judges who are children will be proof of that… If the children don't love a book, it won't win."

Ibrahim, his fellow child judges and Cottrell-Boyce will be joined on the judging panel by Ghosts and Horrible Histories actor Lolly Adefope and award-winning children's book shop owner, Sanchita Basu De Sarkar.

Ibrahim said he loves reading "because it's just a way to unwind yourself from the outside world. If you get stuck in a book, you're not getting your face out of there until you finish it".

He's far too professional to share which books on the list he likes best, but he told me when he was reading one of them recently: "I had to tell my mum to confiscate it because I couldn't stop reading it and I was getting a headache."

Cottrell-Boyce said he isn't concerned over whether the adult judges might dominate the decision-making.

"If - like me - you've been visiting schools as a children's writer for 20 years, it's a rare thing to meet a child who is too over-awed to express an opinion. They're usually very forthright".

Ibrahim proves that point. He told me "the adults are not going to control that meeting… 100% not!"

He's looking for "something that has different perspectives, you can see it in a different way. New characters, not just the same old sloppy characters that authors make all the time. They just make these books that just have the same plot line".

The shortlisted books are by authors from the UK, Ireland, Australia, Italy and Pakistan. Cottrell-Boyce described the list as "full of surprises." Here it is:

The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen by Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts. Readers on Goodreads describe it as "super creepy" and "how horror for kids should be written."

War by Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano. It's the third book in their graphic novel series and tells the story of 14-year old Kat, living under siege in an unnamed European city.

The Night I Borrowed Time by Iqbal Hussain - the British-Pakistani author and former journalist's debut Children's book weaves a story through the eyes of Zubair, a seventh son who has inherited the power of time travel and tries to fix the lives of his family.

The Rambler's Curse by Mikey Please - the fantasy-comedy by the Aardman animator, who has also illustrated the book, has been described by The Guardian as a "laugh-out-loud, shaggy-dog spiral of purposes mistook".

The Teller of Tall Tales by Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston, was a critic's choice in The Daily Telegraph. It's about a grandmother living in a remote cabin who weaves mysterious stories for her estranged grandson.

Tadpole Summer by Catherine Bruton is about a frog whose younger brother is unwell. It's described as a song to nature, family and friendship

Séamus Almost Famous by Jessica Scott-Whyte - this is the Irish author's second book and is illustrated by Becka Moor. Poor Séamus is on a mission to emerge from the shadows of his family - even his baby sister is an accidental internet sensation.

Hometown by Australian Shaun Tan tells the story of a girl living on a distant planet who is one day told by a visitor in a spacesuit that she is actually from somewhere very far away. A review in The Observer called it "perfect fuel for a voracious imagination".

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC the range of subjects was "amazing".

"Children's books can be about anything, can deal with anything. But the tone has to convey hope. I can't think of a darker childhood than the one endured by Anne of Green Gables. I also can't think of a more joyous book than Anne of Green Gables."

He acknowledges the worrying statistics on reading. The National Literacy Trust's Annual Literacy Survey last year showed the percentage of children and young people who said they enjoyed reading was its lowest in 20 years. Just one in three aged eight to 18 said they enjoyed reading in their free time, down by more than a third since 2005.

"That's why we're here! To fight the fight. To make sure our children have as many opportunities as possible to discover how pleasurable, how bonding, how thrilling and enriching and fortifying it can be to slip out of the prison of the present into the infinity of the story."

Ibrahim told me "my friends don't read books at all".

He doesn't try to persuade them. "I let them live their life. I live my life".

But if he were to try to, what would he say?

"Put a timer on your phone, make sure it's blocked and then they'll decide to do something more productive. I might be able to convince them... because it can help you with English, your confidence, and help you build self esteem."

For him, though, the best thing about a book is when it takes him into another world. "If you try to take your head out of it, it makes you think 'oh my god what's going to happen next?'"

The winning book will be announced in February next year at the Young V&A in London. 30,000 copies of the shortlisted books will be given to children who need them most.

A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia

Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.

Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.

But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.

That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.

Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".

Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.

Trunmp and Xi ahead of their meeting in Shenzhen last week

Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.

For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.

Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.

The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.

Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.

But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.

Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.

Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.

The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.

The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.

China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.

Jensen Huang at an Nvidia event in Berlin in October

And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.

He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.

If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.

What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.

Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.

What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.

Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.

Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

Kevin de Bruyne won 16 trophies in 10 years at Manchester City

Kevin de Bruyne's move to Napoli in 2025 was supposed to mark a continuation of his glittering decade at Manchester City as he approaches the twilight years of his career.

Instead, the midfielder, who is widely regarded as one of the stand-out players of his generation, has seen his time in Naples threaten to turn sour amid an early injury, friction with his team-mates and rumours of a January exit.

Napoli were Serie A champions in 2024-25 - the year before De Bruyne's arrival - but are currently languishing in eighth, while they sit 27th in the Champions League after a heavy 4-1 defeat at Porto earlier this month.

Belgium international De Bruyne lifted 16 trophies in his 10 years at City and is guaranteed a generous ovation when he returns to the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday but the highs of his time in England are in contrast to the struggles he is seemingly enduring in Italy.

"Not a lot I can say for the moment," said De Bruyne when asked about his future. "I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

"There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening."

De Bruyne's feelings for Man City will 'never change'

Did Man City let De Bruyne leave too soon?

Statue, Pep's tears & a missed sitter - De Bruyne's emotional farewell

City decided not to renew De Bruyne's contract during the 2024-25 season and the player had the choice of heading to the US with Chicago Fire or staying in one of the top-five leagues in Europe.

The 35-year-old felt he could still cut it at the highest level but his first season at Napoli was heavily disrupted by a hamstring injury which kept him out for more than four months, restricting him to 21 appearances.

Napoli finished runners up to Inter Milan to lose their Serie A title and De Bruyne reportedly said , external he was "happy" manager Antonio Conte had departed in the summer as promises were not kept regarding the style of play.

But despite making his name as a technically gifted number 10, De Bruyne's role has been remodelled into a deeper holding one under Massimiliano Allegri in an ageing squad that has struggled this season.

In Porto, the fractures were clear to see, with De Bruyne having a heated on-field confrontation , external with striker Lorenzo Lucca and his team-mates were forced to step in to diffuse the situation.

The passionate side of De Bruyne's game was shown in Manchester too.

The midfielder shouted "shut up" at manager Pep Guardiola during a Champions League game against Real Madrid in 2023, and said "let me talk" when David Silva and Fernandinho were ushering him off the pitch at half-time shortly after he was booked against Napoli in 2017.

"Speaking about the pitch, De Bruyne is the best player this year at Napoli," Naples-based journalist Vincenzo Credendino tells BBC Sport. "The point is that the whole team is having difficulties.

"We saw that there is a problem, at least between De Bruyne and Lorenzo Lucca. Their acting was very, very clear and I think that in that time, the two of them were wrong.

"On one hand you cannot swear at another team-mate but on the other hand, De Bruyne reproached Lucca without encouraging him, so it was a bad show."

De Bruyne has played 16 times for Napoli this season - contributing four goals and two assists - but his long-term future at the club remains unclear.

In September, De Bruyne's wife reportedly , external told a Belgian publication about their desire to move back home, saying "the sooner we get there, the better" as the player leads a "very restricted life" in Naples.

Asked if the quotes had been misinterpreted, De Bruyne said: "To be honest, I am pretty annoyed because if you read the article, that none of you have read, to understand what she said.

"I was away in Belgium and a lot of noise came and a lot of bad reactions to my wife and family. I saw pictures of my house, I don't think it is OK but it is what it is and some press created this in Italy. I don't know why.

"Nobody knows my life, you will never know. People who work with me are not allowed to say anything but obviously it is something that I take away and think about. It has not been nice for my wife or for my family."

It has led to interest from the Netherlands with PSV Eindhoven making a £1.67m offer to sign him in January, but the two clubs are apart in their valuations as Napoli want up to £6.7m, according to Credendino.

"Napoli fans were not happy [with the interview]," he says. "There are many fans that say, 'OK, you can leave if you want, we are not putting chains on anybody'."

Napoli boss Allegri left the door open for a January exit by saying in his pre-match news conference the pair had "not spoken" about his future and it is "down to the players and who wants to leave" when the transfer window opens.

City manager Enzo Maresca was assistant to Pep Guardiola during the 2022-23 campaign in which De Bruyne helped the club to a Treble of trophies and the Italian has fond memories of the "fantastic season" they spent together.

"No doubt, [he is] one of the best," Maresca said of De Bruyne in his pre-match news conference. "Not only personally but also for the history of this club. In the last 10 years all the trophies the club achieved Kevin was here.

"He was an important player, a top guy, polite and for me it was a pleasure to work with him."

This is not the first time De Bruyne will be facing his former club with a reunion with City in the Champions League last season.

That trip turned out to be a bitterly unhappy experience, with De Bruyne substituted after 26 minutes following Giovanni di Lorenzo's red card in the 2-0 defeat.

The midfielder will be hoping for a better result on Tuesday as he aims to park his struggles for one evening.

City and Belgium winger Jeremy Doku said: "Kevin is someone that likes football. Even at this age he loves it.

"I don't have any doubts about his quality and I am sure everything will be fine in Napoli."
